summary: This unit teaches you to find, record, protect and make money from a business's intangible assets: brands, copyright, patents, trade secrets, know-how, customer relationships, reputation and digital assets. You will learn how each is protected, how to use contracts and good practice, how to respond to infringement, and how to use licensing and franchising, with the sums involved.

blocks.p: Most people think of a business's assets as things they can touch: buildings, vehicles, machines, stock. But much of the value of a modern business lies in things you cannot touch: its **brand and reputation**, its **recipes and designs**, its **software and website**, its **customer lists** and the **know-how** of its staff. These are **intangible assets**. They are often copied, lost or given away by accident. This unit is for managers who must identify them, protect them and use them to earn more.

Many of these assets are covered by **intellectual property (IP)** rights: copyright, trade marks, patents, industrial designs and similar rights. Some are protected by registration, some arise automatically, and some (such as trade secrets and know-how) are protected only by keeping them secret and by contracts. A manager needs to know which protection suits which asset.

A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms such as trade mark, patent, royalty, licensor, NDA, amortisation) and longer answers.
**Group practical tasks**: an audit of a firm's intangible assets with a register and action plan, and the preparation and negotiation of a brand licensing proposal.

blocks.note: This unit explains general business practice. Laws on IP differ by country and change. For a real dispute, registration or contract, a manager takes advice from an attorney who deals with intellectual property.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **asset** is something a business owns or controls that has value. A **tangible** asset has physical form. An **intangible** asset does not. You cannot protect what you have not identified, so the first job is to find and list them.

blocks.h: How to carry out an audit

flow: Explain to managers what intangible assets are and why they matter
Meet each department: marketing, production, sales, human resources, finance and legal
List every asset found and who created or owns it
Check the paperwork: registrations, contracts, licences, renewal dates
Rank each asset by importance to the business and risk of loss
Record all of it in a register
List gaps and risks and write an action plan with owners, costs and dates

blocks.p: A **register of intangible assets** is a spreadsheet or database. Its purpose is to track ownership, protection and renewals. It does not replace the fixed asset register, which records physical assets and their depreciation. A useful register has these columns:

head: Column
Why it is needed
rows: Asset and type
Says what it is: brand, copyright, trade secret, domain name, and so on
Owner
The firm, a staff member, a contractor or a partner. Wrong ownership is a common hidden risk.
Current protection
Registered, contract, secrecy, access control, or none
Registration or licence details and renewal date
Rights lapse if renewal fees are missed; a domain name expires if not renewed
Importance
How much the business would lose without it
Risk
How easily it could be copied, lost or misused
Action and owner
What must be done, by whom and by when

blocks.note: Assets are often hidden in other people's hands: a logo owned by the designer who drew it, a website address registered in a former employee's name, a social media account that only one person can log in to. An audit looks for these.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Different assets need different protection. Learn what each right covers, how it arises, and what it does not cover.

head: Right
Protects
How it arises
Notes
rows: **Copyright**
Original works: writing, music, photographs, films, drawings, software code, website content
Automatically when the work is created and recorded in some form. Registration is not usually needed.
Protects the way an idea is expressed, not the idea itself. Lasts for a long period set by law.
**Trade mark**
A name, logo, slogan or other sign that distinguishes a firm's goods or services
By use, but strongest when **registered** with the national intellectual property office
Registration can be renewed for as long as the mark is used. It covers the country where registered, so register in each export market.
**Patent**
A new, inventive and industrially useful invention (a product or process)
By application and grant after examination. The invention must be new, so do not publish it before filing.
Gives the owner the sole right to use it for a limited period, typically up to about 20 years. Details are public.
**Industrial design**
The appearance of a product: its shape, pattern or ornament
By registration
Protects the look, not how the product works.
**Geographical indication**
The name of a place used for products with a quality or reputation from that place
By registration or special law
Stops others using the place name for products not from there.
**Trade secret / confidential information**
Valuable information, such as a recipe, formula or customer list, that is kept secret
Not by registration. It lasts only while it stays secret.
Protected by secrecy, access control and contracts. Once public it is lost.

Best protection
rows: Company logo
Trade mark (and copyright in the artwork, owned by the firm if properly assigned)

Copyright

Distinctive new shape of a chair

blocks.p: Registration costs money and takes time, and a small firm cannot protect everything. Rank assets by **value and risk of loss** and protect the most important first. Registering everything ever created wastes money; waiting for a rival to copy something is too late.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, the national body for registering trade marks, patents and designs and for guidance on copyright is the Jamaica Intellectual Property Office (JIPO). Jamaica protects some place names as geographical indications, such as the name of a famous mountain-grown product. A manager checks current rules with JIPO or an attorney. Jamaican registration does not protect a brand in the United States, Canada or the United Kingdom: for export markets, register there too.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Who owns an intangible asset is decided by the law and by contracts. Not knowing the answer is one of the most common and expensive mistakes.

ul: When an employee creates a work **as part of the job**, such as writing training software, the **employer** usually owns the copyright, unless the contract says otherwise.
Include in every employment contract a **confidentiality clause**, and a clause that work created in the course of employment belongs to the firm.
In some senior posts a reasonable restriction on approaching customers after leaving may be added, if allowed by employment law. Take legal advice on wording.
Explain the firm's intangible assets during induction, and limit access to sensitive information to those who need it.
When someone leaves, end system access, recover devices and papers, and remind them of their confidentiality duties.

blocks.p: A freelancer who is not an employee often **keeps the copyright** in what he or she creates unless the contract gives it to the client. When a firm pays a designer for a logo, the contract must say that the rights in the logo are **assigned** (transferred) to the firm. A contract saying nothing, or letting the designer reuse the logo freely, leaves the firm with a logo it may not own.

A **non-disclosure agreement (NDA)**, also called a confidentiality agreement, is a signed promise to keep shared information secret and to use it only for an agreed purpose. Sign one **before** showing a new product design to a possible manufacturing partner, an investor or a supplier. A spoken promise is hard to prove.

When two firms will develop something together, agree **before** starting who will own the new IP, who may use it and for what, and what happens if the partnership ends. Disputes arise when this is left until the product is finished.
Contracts with agents, distributors and suppliers should say that the firm's brand and materials remain the firm's property, how they may be used and what happens when the contract ends.

blocks.note: A patent application needs the invention to be new. If the inventor shows it in public, posts it online or describes it without a confidentiality agreement before filing, she may lose the right to a patent. Keep careful notes and drawings, get advice and file first.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Digital assets, reputation, know-how and customer relationships

ul: **Domain name**: register it in the **firm's own name**, not in a staff member's or web designer's name. Set automatic renewal and send reminders to a named manager. If the address expires, someone else may register it. Consider registering common misspellings and similar names.

**Social media accounts**: open them in the firm's name with passwords held securely by the firm, two-step login on, and at least two authorised administrators. The firm, not the person who set them up, controls them.

**Software**: buy proper licences and keep a record of them. Unofficial copies expose the firm to legal action and to malware. One licence may not be shared among all staff unless the licence allows it.
**Websites and content**: keep copies of the files and records of who created them and the terms.

**Databases and customer lists**: limit access, use passwords, back up securely. A customer list also holds **personal data**, so the data protection law applies: collect only what you need, keep it secure and use it for a clear purpose.

blocks.p: **Reputation** is what customers believe about a firm. **Goodwill** is the value of that reputation and customer loyalty, shown most clearly when a business is sold for more than its physical assets are worth. A hotel that gets many poor reviews about cleanliness puts its reputation at risk. Protect reputation by reliable service, monitoring feedback and reviews, replying to complaints quickly and politely, and having a plan for who speaks for the business in a crisis.

**Know-how** is practical knowledge: how to run a key process, how to set a machine, how to prepare a product. If a senior technician who knows a key process is about to retire, the best step is to have him **document and teach it**: write procedures, take photographs or short videos, pair him with younger staff, and store the records as company documents.

Long-term customer relationships are valuable. Protect them with good records, good service, more than one person knowing each key account (so that you are not dependent on one salesperson) and clear contracts. If a sales manager leaves to join a rival, end his access, recover devices and company records, and remind him of his duties.

ul: Before launching a new product name, **search existing trade marks** so you do not use a name that someone else already owns.
Do not use photographs, music or text from the internet in your brochures unless you have permission or a licence. Internet images are not free simply because they are online.
Buy proper software licences. A cheap copy from an unofficial seller is a risk, not a saving.

blocks.p: **Infringement** is the use of someone else's intellectual property without permission. A firm that owns valuable IP must watch for it, since the owner, not the state, is normally responsible for noticing misuse.

ul: Check markets, shops and online sellers regularly for copies of your brand or designs.
Search for your brand name and logo online; set alerts.
Watch the trade mark register for new applications that look like yours.
Ask staff, agents and customers to report suspected copies.

flow: Collect evidence: dated screenshots, photographs, copies of listings, a test purchase
Check your own records: what you own, where it is registered and until when
Take advice from an attorney who deals with intellectual property
Usually the first formal step is a lawyer's letter asking the other party to stop
If it continues, consider further steps with the attorney: negotiation, a complaint to the online platform, or court action
Record the outcome and fix the weakness that allowed it

blocks.note: Never seize goods by force, post the person's photograph as a thief, or ignore the problem. Collect evidence and take advice. Small copying left unchallenged can grow and may weaken your rights.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: If copies are sold from a website overseas, the rules and the best route depend on that country. Check where your rights are registered, and take advice. Platform complaints, a letter to the seller and customs notices may all be options.

sections.title: Using intangible assets to earn income

blocks.p: A **licence** gives another person the right to use your IP on agreed terms while **you keep ownership**. The owner is the **licensor**; the user is the **licensee**. The licensee pays a **royalty**, usually a percentage of sales or a fee per unit. A licence gives the firm income without the cost of making and selling everything itself. It is not a sale, and it does not remove the need to watch for misuse.
A brand licence agreement should set out:

ul: **Territory**: where the licensee may sell.
**Products**: exactly what may carry the brand.
**Term**: how long the licence lasts, and how it can be renewed or ended.
**Royalty rate, minimum payment and payment dates.**
**Quality standards** and the licensor's right to inspect.
**Reporting and audit**: sales reports and the right to check them.
**How the brand may be used** and who may approve packaging.
**What happens at the end**: stocks, rights and returned materials.

blocks.p: The licensor must check quality because a poor-quality product sold under its brand **damages the brand's reputation**.

J$800,000 is due

blocks.p: A **franchise** lets others trade under your brand, using your recipes and system, in return for fees. The franchisee pays an initial fee and ongoing royalties, and invests in the premises. The franchisor needs less capital and grows faster. The risk is that one badly run outlet can damage the brand, so the franchisor must train, inspect and control quality.

rows: 6 franchisees each paying a yearly fee of J$450,000
Each franchisee also pays 5% of yearly sales of J$18,000,000
J$900,000 per franchisee
Total royalties from the 6

blocks.h: Licence or invest yourself? A worked comparison

blocks.p: A firm can license its brand abroad for a royalty of 5% of sales of J$40,000,000 a year for 3 years (J$2,000,000 a year, J$6,000,000 in all, with almost no investment), or invest J$9,000,000 in its own production, expecting profit of J$3,000,000 a year. Own production earns J$9,000,000 over 3 years, minus J$9,000,000 invested: **J$0**. On these figures, the licence gives a better and safer return, but the owner keeps less control. Always compare return, risk and control, not return alone.

A **user licence** for software gives the customer the right to use it on agreed terms. It does not give ownership of the copyright, or the right to resell copies or sell changed versions of the code.

sections.title: Valuing intangible assets and reviewing the portfolio

blocks.p: A firm may need a value when it **sells or buys** a business, **licenses** rights, **borrows** against assets, brings in a partner, settles an infringement claim or decides how much to spend on protection. Valuing intangible assets is difficult because they are unique, their future income is uncertain and a self-built brand is hard to measure reliably. This is why a brand a firm built itself is usually **not shown as an asset on its balance sheet**.

When a firm buys a business for more than the fair value of its net assets, the difference is **goodwill**. Worked example: a firm buys a printing business for J$30,000,000. The fair value of its net assets is J$22,500,000. Goodwill = 30,000,000 − 22,500,000 = **J$7,500,000**. Check: 22,500,000 + 7,500,000 = 30,000,000.

**Amortisation** spreads the cost of an intangible asset with a limited life over that life, in the same way that depreciation spreads the cost of equipment. Straight-line method: (cost − value at the end) ÷ number of years.

Worked example: a software licence costs J$2,400,000, will be used for 5 years and will have no value at the end. Yearly charge = 2,400,000 ÷ 5 = **J$480,000**. After 2 years, the amount still to be charged (carrying amount) is 2,400,000 − (2 × 480,000) = **J$1,440,000**.

ul: Update the register: new assets, changed owners, expired items.
Check renewal dates and pay fees on time.
Decide for each right: **keep, license or drop**. A trade mark that the firm stopped using five years ago should not be renewed automatically. It could be lapsed, licensed or sold.
Check that contracts, access controls and staff training are up to date.
Look for new assets created during the year and protect them early.

blocks.p: Staff training matters. Staff who understand the firm's intangible assets protect and use them properly. They must not register assets in their own names or take them to rivals.

ul: I can explain what intangible assets are and list the main groups.
I can carry out an audit and keep a register that shows owner, protection, renewal date, importance and risk.
I can match copyright, trade marks, patents, designs, geographical indications and trade secrets to the right asset.
I can say who owns work created by employees and freelancers, and what contracts must say.
I can use confidentiality agreements and sensible access controls.
I can protect domain names, social media accounts, software and databases.
I can explain goodwill, reputation and know-how and how to protect them.
I can monitor for infringement, collect evidence and take the first steps.
I can explain licensing and franchising, with royalty and fee calculations.
I can work out goodwill and straight-line amortisation.
I can review a portfolio and decide to keep, license or drop each right.

terms: Intangible asset
An asset with no physical form, such as a brand, know-how or customer list.
Intellectual property (IP)
Legal rights over creations of the mind, such as copyright, trade marks and patents.
Copyright
The right that protects original works from the moment they are created.
Trade mark
A sign that distinguishes a firm's goods or services from others.
Patent
The sole right to use a new invention for a limited period.
Industrial design
Protection for the appearance of a product.
Geographical indication
A place name protected for products from that place.
Trade secret
Valuable information protected by keeping it confidential.
NDA
Non-disclosure agreement: a signed promise to keep information secret.
Infringement
Use of someone's IP without permission.
Licence
Permission to use IP on agreed terms; the owner keeps ownership.
Licensor / licensee
The owner who grants a licence / the user who receives it.
Royalty
A payment to the owner for each sale or use under a licence.
Franchise
A right to trade under a firm's brand and system in return for fees.
Goodwill
The value of reputation and customer loyalty, seen when a business is sold.
Amortisation
Spreading the cost of an intangible asset over its useful life.
Domain name
The registered website address of a business.

c1.title: A Mandeville herbal tea company
c1.text: Camille Lewis owns a herbal tea company in Mandeville. Her best-selling blend uses a mix of leaves that only she and two senior packers know. The company name and a leaf logo have been used for eight years but are not registered. A former packer has begun selling a similar blend in nearby markets in a package that looks very like Camille's. Camille has no written record of her intangible assets.

c2.title: A Kingston software start-up
c2.text: A Kingston start-up develops a scheduling app for clinics. Its founder, Mr Winston Beckford, paid a freelance developer to write part of the code and paid a designer for the app's logo. Neither contract mentions ownership. A major bank wants to see the product before agreeing to a partnership. The firm's website address was registered by the web designer in her own name and expires next month.

c3.title: A Portland skin-care brand goes abroad
c3.text: A Portland company makes coconut-oil skin care under a registered brand. A manufacturer in Barbados wants a licence to make and sell the products in the Eastern Caribbean. The Barbadian firm expects sales of J$25,000,000 a year and offers a royalty of 4% of sales. The Portland owner, Ms Patrice Gordon, worries that cheaper ingredients might damage the brand.

c4.title: A Kingston fashion label
c4.text: A Kingston fashion label has registered its name and logo and owns the designs of its dresses. An online seller based in another country is offering dresses that look the same under a near-identical name. A marketing assistant has also taken a photograph from a photographer's website for a brochure. The studio uses an unofficial copy of design software bought cheaply from a seller at a market.

c5.title: A St Ann restaurant group
c5.text: A St Ann restaurant group wants to grow by franchising its brand and recipes to six owners in other towns. The group has also just bought a small bakery for J$30,000,000. The bakery's net assets have a fair value of J$22,500,000. The group's social media pages were opened by a marketing agency that holds the passwords. The group paid J$2,400,000 for a point-of-sale software licence to be used for 5 years.

questions.q: Which form of protection best suits Camille's secret blend of leaves?
o: A patent, since the blend is a valuable and original product
Trade secret, with confidentiality terms and limited access
Copyright in the written list of leaves used in the blend
A geographical indication for the name of the blend's product
questions.why: A recipe is protected by keeping it secret and controlling who knows it. A patent would require publishing it, and copyright protects expression, not a recipe. A geographical indication is for place names.

questions.q: Camille's name and logo are used but not registered. What should she do?
o: Rely on use alone, since eight years of use is enough
Change the logo every year so that copies are easier to see
Keep the name and logo off the packaging to avoid being copied
Register them as trade marks, the strongest protection
questions.why: Registration gives the clearest and strongest right to stop others using a similar name or logo. Use helps but is harder to prove. Changing or removing the brand weakens the business.

questions.q: A former packer sells a similar blend in near-identical packaging. What should Camille do first?
o: Collect dated evidence and take legal advice
Confront him at the market and seize his stock
Post his photograph online and call him a thief
Do nothing, as one small seller will do little harm
questions.why: Evidence and advice come first. Force or public accusation can create liability for Camille, and doing nothing allows copying to grow. The next step is usually a letter from her attorney.

questions.q: Which step would best prevent Camille depending on three people for the blend's know-how?
o: Ask the three packers to keep the process safely in their heads
Promise the three packers a bonus if the blend is never copied
Record the process, store it securely and train other staff
Reduce the number of people who pack the tea in each week
questions.why: Know-how that is only in people's heads leaves with them. Documenting and teaching it, with confidentiality terms in contracts, protects continuity. Fewer packers or a bonus do not solve the dependence.

questions.q: The freelance developer's contract does not mention ownership of the code. What is the likely position?
o: The firm owns the code automatically because it paid for the work
The government copyright office owns it until the code is registered
The developer may own it unless it was assigned in writing
Mr Beckford owns it personally, since he founded the firm
questions.why: A freelancer who is not an employee usually keeps copyright unless the contract assigns it. Payment alone does not always transfer ownership. The firm should obtain a written assignment now.

questions.q: What should Mr Beckford do before showing the app to the bank?
o: Have the bank sign a confidentiality agreement
Post the app's design online to show it is the firm's own work
Ask the bank to promise orally not to share it
Send the design by ordinary post without any covering letter
questions.why: An NDA signed before disclosure gives a clear, provable duty of confidence. An oral promise is hard to prove, and posting the design publicly could destroy secrecy.

questions.q: The firm's website address, registered in the web designer's name, expires next month. What should Mr Beckford do?
o: Let the address expire and buy a new address later on
Ask the designer to keep renewing it each year at her own cost
Wait to see whether anyone else tries to register the address
Move it into the firm's name and set up renewal
questions.why: Domain names should be registered in the firm's own name, with automatic renewal and reminders to a named manager. If an address expires, another person may register it.

questions.q: Which action best protects the firm's customer database of clinics?
o: Email a copy of the list to every member of staff at the firm
Limit access, set passwords and keep secure back-ups
Store it on a shared office computer without any password
Print a copy and keep it on the desk at the reception
questions.why: Limiting access with passwords and secure backup protects a valuable asset. The database also holds personal data, which the data protection law requires the firm to keep secure.

questions.q: What royalty would the Barbadian manufacturer owe in a year at J$25,000,000 of sales and 4%?
Over a 3-year licence at the same sales level, how much royalty income would Ms Gordon receive?
questions.why: 1,000,000 × 3 = J$3,000,000. A yearly royalty must be multiplied by the number of years in the term.

questions.q: Ms Gordon worries about cheaper ingredients. What should the licence agreement include?
o: Quality standards, inspection and a right to end the licence
A promise by the manufacturer that it will try its very best always
A clause allowing the manufacturer to change the recipe freely
A rule that no sales reports are needed from the manufacturer
questions.why: Quality control is essential, because poor products under the brand harm its reputation. Standards, inspection rights and termination rights give the licensor real control. Good intentions or free changes do not.

questions.q: What is the main benefit to Ms Gordon of licensing rather than selling the brand?
o: She hands over all responsibility for the brand for ever
She stops needing to watch for misuse of the brand
She earns income while keeping ownership of the brand
She no longer has to pay renewal fees on the registration
questions.why: A licence gives income and keeps ownership. It does not remove the need to protect and monitor the brand or pay renewals, which remain the owner's duty.

questions.q: The marketing assistant used a photograph from a photographer's website in a brochure. What should the manager do?
o: Get permission or a licence, or use a licensed image
Keep using it, since pictures found online are free to use
Use it, provided that the colours are changed a little
Use it, provided that the brochure is only a small one
questions.why: Images found online are usually protected by copyright. Use needs permission or a licence. Altering the colours or keeping the brochure small does not change that.

questions.q: The studio uses an unofficial copy of design software bought cheaply. What should the label do?
o: Keep using it, since it saves money
Use it only for small jobs
Buy a proper licence and stop using the copy
Share it among all staff to spread the saving
questions.why: Unlicensed software breaches the owner's rights and risks legal action and malware. The firm should respect others' rights by buying proper licences.

questions.q: What is the best first step against the overseas seller who copies the label's dresses and name?
o: Report the seller to the Jamaican tax authority for selling abroad
Collect evidence and take advice from an IP attorney
Copy the seller's own website design in return, to show the harm
Wait for the seller to stop selling the copies on its own
questions.why: Rights and remedies depend on the country, so advice is needed. Evidence should include dated screenshots of the listings. Tax reports, copying back or waiting are not effective.

questions.q: Why should the label also register its name in the countries where it sells online?
o: Jamaican registration is cancelled when a firm starts selling abroad
Overseas registration is free of charge for Jamaican firms
Registration abroad removes the need for any written contracts
Registration covers only the country where it is made
questions.why: Trade mark registration covers only the country in which it is registered (or a group of countries under a special system). To block copies in another market, register there as well.

questions.q: What is the goodwill on the bakery purchase?
questions.why: Goodwill = price − fair value of net assets = 30,000,000 − 22,500,000 = J$7,500,000.

questions.q: What is the yearly amortisation charge on the J$2,400,000 software licence, with no value at the end?
questions.why: 2,400,000 ÷ 5 = J$480,000 a year. Amortisation spreads the cost over the useful life.

questions.q: Each of the six franchisees will pay 5% of yearly sales of J$18,000,000. What are the royalties from one franchisee in a year?
questions.why: 18,000,000 × 5 ÷ 100 = J$900,000. J$5,400,000 would be the total from all six franchisees.

questions.q: The marketing agency holds the passwords to the social media pages. What should the group do?
o: Let the agency keep control, because it set the accounts up first
Share the passwords with every member of staff in the group
Move the accounts to the group, with two administrators
Close the accounts and open new accounts every single year
questions.why: The firm should control accounts that carry its brand, with secure passwords, two-step login and at least two authorised administrators, so that it keeps control if people or agencies change.
